title: Prediction surface
opening: A target says what you want. A prediction records what you expect, what you based it on and how you will find out whether it happened.

labels.comparison: A target and a prediction answer different questions
labels.comparisonIntro: A teacher wants learners to choose a method in a new case after revising an example. Compare what can be learned from a target alone and from a dated prediction.
labels.comparisonDisclosure: This is a hypothetical classroom example. The outcome buttons show possible results; no learner result is reported here.
labels.targetText: Learners choose the method in a new case.
labels.targetEffect: This names the result the teacher wants. It does not say what the teacher expects to happen or what evidence supports that expectation.
labels.predictionText: Before revising the example, the teacher expects learners to choose the method in a new case at the next check.
labels.predictionEffect: Keep the date, evidence cutoff, assumptions and resolution condition with this expectation. That record lets the later observation test the original prediction.
labels.outcomePrompt: Choose a possible result to compare with the preserved prediction.
labels.selected: Learners chose the method in a new case
labels.missed: Learners did not choose the method in a new case
labels.missLabel: Learners did not choose the method
labels.selectedEffect: In this hypothetical branch, the specified result occurred. Compare it with the preserved prediction, then check whether the revision changes the work in other cases.
labels.missedEffect: In this hypothetical branch, the specified result did not occur. Keep the original prediction beside the observation; use the gap to decide what to revise and what to check next.
labels.practice: Write a prediction you can check
labels.practiceIntro: Use a real decision. Record when you will check, the evidence and its latest date, assumptions and plausible results, what would settle the prediction, early signs to watch and what would make you update it. Compare acting, leaving things alone and gathering more information, including what success might break and the next constraint. Afterward, compare the result with the prediction you preserved.
labels.private: This private note is optional. The six required course questions are separate.
labels.length: This prediction is over 2,000 characters. Shorten it to save; your text stays here.
labels.sourceQuote:
Before trying the change, write what you expect to happen and when you will check it. Name the result you are predicting, the evidence you have used and the latest point that evidence covers. State the assumptions and an expected range or several possible results. Decide what observation will settle the prediction, what early signs you will watch and what would make you update it. Keep this dated prediction so you can compare it with the result instead of remembering a different expectation afterward. These records form the prediction surface.

Compare acting, leaving things alone and gathering more information. Include what success might break, the next constraint and how other agents may respond. When combining judgments, inspect shared sources and assumptions; several versions of the same reasoning do not supply independent evidence.
labels.sourceDisclosure: The source text is preserved. The classroom example and interactive comparison are authored teaching expansions, not observed outcomes.

feedback.unavailable: Private saving is unavailable. Your prediction stays on screen.
feedback.length: Shorten the prediction to fit the 2,000-character limit. Your text stays here.
feedback.conflict: This prediction changed elsewhere. Your text remains here; compare the saved version before saving again.
feedback.readFailure: The saved prediction could not be loaded.
feedback.readbackFailure: The save could not be confirmed. Retry to check the same save.
feedback.saveFailure: The save is uncertain. Retry to check the same save.
feedback.retryPending: The earlier save is unresolved. Retry the same prediction before changing it.

example: Hypothetical teaching example. Before revising the example, I expect learners to choose the method in a new case at the next class check. Evidence cutoff: the current exercise and learner responses reviewed on [date]. Assumptions: the new case tests the same choice without repeating the revised example. Resolve by recording whether each learner chooses the method in that case. Update earlier if the new case tests something different or the exercise changes again.

source.assessmentBoundary: Six required open-ended course questions remain separate from the optional private prediction. No qualified semantic grade or learner outcome is supplied.
